conclusion.justification: The report concludes that the claim is largely supported and generally true, though it notes the benefits are conditional and depend on external factors like noise, temperature, and whether a window or door is opened.
conclusion.label: leans_endorse

report:
The evidence suggests the claim is largely supported, though conditionally rather than universally true.

Controlled research points consistently in one direction: lower CO2 concentrations from ventilation correlate with better sleep. A field intervention study from DTU/Aalto researchers with 27 subjects found that opening a bedroom **window** (not just a door) reduced CO2, and both objectively measured and subjectively rated sleep quality improved compared to closed conditions. Notably, opening just the door reduced CO2 but did not produce the same sleep benefits (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605). A related cross-sectional study confirmed that enhanced ventilation via window or door opening improved subjectively-assessed sleep quality and perceived air quality (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322007879). Follow-up work from DTU further specified thresholds: keeping CO2 below ~750-1000 ppm through ventilation allows air quality good enough that it doesn't impair sleep, and better ventilation was linked to improved next-day cognitive performance (https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day).

However, the effect is conditional, not absolute. A Shanghai study cited by the Sleep Foundation found that while open windows improved air quality, sleep still suffered—likely because summer conditions made bedrooms hotter and noisier, offsetting air-quality gains (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed). This indicates outdoor temperature, noise, and pollution levels can negate or reverse the benefit.

**Conclusion:** The claim is not false—it's an oversimplification. Under good outdoor conditions (cool, quiet, clean air), opening a window improves ventilation, lowers CO2, and measurably improves sleep quality. But if outdoor air is hot, noisy, or polluted, opening a window can worsen sleep despite improving air quality. The mechanism (door vs. window) also matters, as doors alone were less effective. So the claim is generally true but context-dependent rather than universally false.
